ABLD: Real asset companies, energy producers and pipelines alongside property owners, chosen for strong free cash flow relative to the capital in the business. It is an income-leaning bet on physical assets, so it moves with energy prices and property markets more than with the broad stock market.
AIFR: Semiconductor foundries: the contract factories in Taiwan, the US and elsewhere that manufacture chips designed by other companies. It is a focused bet on chipmaking capacity rather than chip design, so it depends on global demand for outsourced manufacturing and on heavy spending for new plants.
BTCI: Income built on bitcoin: the fund holds bitcoin funds and sells options on them, turning part of bitcoin's wild price movement into regular payouts. The options cap some of the upside, and the downside is still bitcoin's, so payouts come with big swings in the fund's price.
CEF: Physical gold and silver bullion held together in one trust, so the shares follow the prices of both precious metals at once. Gold is the steadier store of value and silver the swingier industrial metal, and the blend sits between Sprott's single-metal trusts in how hard it moves.
FBYY: An income fund built on options tied to a leveraged fund linked to Meta Platforms, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, rather than owning the stock itself. It aims to pay frequent distributions, but the leveraged options structure swings sharply, so it fits short holding periods more than steady investing.
FFLC: Large US companies picked by Fidelity's analysts company by company, blending growth and value names across industries, with technology and internet giants currently prominent. It is a core-style holding whose results rest on fundamental research rather than a formula, so it can drift from the index for long stretches.
FFLG: Large US growth companies picked by Fidelity's analysts company by company, currently led by chipmakers, internet platforms and drug companies. It is a growth holding built on fundamental research, so it will rise and fall harder than the broad market when big growth stocks swing.
FFSM: Small and midsize US companies picked by Fidelity's analysts from the bottom up, company by company, rather than by formula. The mix ranges across industries, and smaller companies swing more than large ones, so this is a growth holding whose results depend heavily on the stock pickers' judgment.
GARP: US companies that pass a quality screen and offer growth at a reasonable price, meaning solid finances without the steepest valuations. At the moment the mix leans toward technology and chipmakers, so it is a growth-leaning core holding that tries to avoid the most expensive corners of the market.
GMAC: A global macro fund that can bet for or against stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities anywhere in the world, based on the managers' read of economies and valuations. Nothing about its mix is fixed, so it can move very differently from a normal portfolio, for better or worse.
GSWO: Stocks from around the world, weighted by four ActiveBeta factors, value, momentum, quality and low volatility, instead of by company size alone. It is a core-style global holding built to tilt toward the traits Goldman believes pay off, so it will not move exactly with the world market.
HFIX: High yield corporate bonds, the below-investment-grade kind that pay extra interest to make up for weaker borrowers, chosen for total return rather than yield alone. It aims to earn more than a plain Treasury fund, but these bonds fall when investors worry about defaults.
HFSI: An income fund that roams across bond types, government and mortgage bonds alongside corporate and riskier debt, shifting the mix as the managers see value. It aims to pay more than a plain government bond fund, and the price of that extra yield is more movement when credit markets wobble.
IROC: High yield municipal bonds: tax-exempt debt from riskier local borrowers such as hospitals, utilities and development projects that must pay more to borrow. The interest is generally free of federal tax, but weaker borrowers mean more price movement and some default risk.
KYC: Digital banking and fintech infrastructure: payment networks, app-based banks and the software firms that run modern finance behind the scenes. It is a focused bet on banking moving to phones and software, split between financial companies and technology firms, so it swings with both sectors.
LLMA: Companies that build large language models, the AI systems behind chatbots: the firms researching, training and deploying their own models and products built on them. It is a focused bet on the model makers themselves rather than the wider AI supply chain, so it rides a young and fast-changing field.
MN: Just six companies: Meta, Anthropic, Nvidia, Google, OpenAI and SpaceX, a handpicked set of the biggest names in social media, chips and artificial intelligence. Three of them are not publicly traded, so exposure comes partly through derivatives, making this an extremely concentrated bet on a few giants.
NECK: The bottleneck suppliers of the AI buildout: makers of memory chips, optical networking gear and other scarce parts that data centers cannot do without. It skips the famous AI names to own the chokepoints instead, so it is a focused, fast-swinging bet on one supply chain.
NUIB: Investment-grade bonds chosen for impact: government, corporate and mortgage bonds whose proceeds fund projects meant to do measurable environmental or social good. It still behaves like a core bond fund, paying interest and cushioning stock swings, with the bond picking screened for impact on top.
NVDW: An income strategy wrapped around one stock, Nvidia, the AI chip leader, using options and Treasury bills rather than simply holding shares. It aims to pay distributions weekly, and the trade-off is that everything rides on one very volatile stock, with options capping some of its biggest jumps.
OAKL: A concentrated handful of US stocks that Oakmark's managers judge to be trading well below what the businesses are worth. With few holdings it is a high-conviction value bet, so it can trail the market for long stretches when cheap stocks stay out of favor.
OVQ: The Nasdaq 100's big growth companies, technology-led, with an options overlay on top that sells options to generate extra income. The overlay trades some of the index's upside for payouts, so it behaves like a slightly tamer, income-paying version of a very growth-heavy fund.
PFRX: A focused portfolio of US stocks drawn from Putnam's own analyst research, concentrating on the team's highest-conviction ideas across industries. With fewer holdings than a broad fund, each pick matters more, so results depend on the analysts' calls rather than on the market as a whole.
PHYS: Actual gold bullion held in vaults, so the shares move with the price of gold itself rather than with mining companies. It is a direct way to own the metal as a safe-haven asset, and it tends to be steadier than silver or gold miners, though it still follows gold's price swings.
POMG: Growth companies in the small and midsize range, actively hunted by PRIMECAP, a manager known for patient, research-driven stock picking. It aims for tomorrow's large companies before they are obvious, so it accepts years of uneven results and bigger swings than a large-company fund.
PSLV: Actual silver bullion held in vaults, so the shares move with the price of the metal itself rather than with mining companies. It is a direct way to own silver as a store of value, and silver swings more than gold because it is also an industrial metal.
RINK: Bonds from many sectors at once, corporate, government, mortgage and riskier high yield among them, with the mix shifted as conditions change. Russell builds it from several specialist bond managers, so it works as a one-fund bond core whose bets are spread across styles.
RTHY: Inflation-protected US Treasury bonds with at least twenty years left to run, whose principal rises with inflation so the payments keep their buying power. The long maturities make the price very sensitive to interest rates, so this protects against inflation while still swinging a lot.
SHYM: Short-term, high yield municipal bonds, actively picked from riskier borrowers such as cities, hospitals and project issuers that pay higher interest because their credit is weaker. The interest is generally free of federal tax, and short maturities limit how much the price moves when interest rates change.
SPPP: Physical platinum and palladium held in vaults, two rarer precious metals used heavily in catalytic converters and industry. Their prices depend more on car production and mining supply than on investors, so they can swing sharply and move very differently from gold.
STYL: Lifestyle brands: clothing, footwear, sports cars and premium labels that sell an image as much as a product, almost all consumer discretionary companies. It is a focused bet on brand power and consumer taste, so it does well when shoppers feel flush and suffers when they trade down.
TETH: Direct exposure to ether, the cryptocurrency of the Ethereum network, held as the fund's asset rather than through futures contracts. Ether's price swings hard with crypto sentiment and with activity on the network, so this is a simple but volatile way to hold it in a brokerage account.
TKNS: A basket of crypto funds holding bitcoin, ethereum, solana and newer tokens, actively shifted between them by the manager rather than fixed in place. It gives one-ticker access to a spread of digital assets, but crypto prices swing violently, so the whole fund moves far more than a stock portfolio.
TLCE: Large US companies across every major industry, actively picked by Thrivent's managers rather than held in index order. It is meant to work as a core stock holding, and its results depend on the managers' picks beating the big-company market over time.
TOPW: A basket of Roundhill's weekly-pay funds, each built on options around a single famous stock such as a chipmaker or a tech giant, gathered into one ticker. It aims for weekly distributions from many names at once, but every ingredient is a leveraged, single-stock strategy, so the swings stay large.
TRIL: The world's trillion-dollar companies: the handful of giant firms, mostly US technology names, big enough to be worth over a trillion dollars each. Owning them in one fund is a concentrated bet on mega-cap dominance, so it swings with a short list of stocks rather than the broad market.
TRPA: The safest slice of collateralized loan obligations: AAA-rated bundles of corporate loans, where many company loans are pooled and this fund holds the tranche paid first. It is an income fund designed to pay more than Treasury bonds while taking the most protected seat in the loan pool.
TRUI: Industrial companies across the sector: machinery makers, aerospace firms, electrical equipment builders and transport suppliers, actively picked rather than index-weighted. It is a focused bet on factories, construction and infrastructure spending, so it does best when the industrial economy is humming.
TRUM: Materials companies: chemical makers, miners and industrial gas producers, actively picked across the sector, with a small slice of consumer firms alongside. It is a focused bet on the raw ingredients of the economy, so it rises and falls with construction, manufacturing and commodity prices.
TRUN: Energy companies across the business: oil and gas producers, refiners and pipeline operators, actively picked across the whole sector. It is a focused bet on fuel prices and energy demand, so it does well when oil is expensive and struggles when crude falls.
TRUR: Real estate companies: landlords of apartments, offices, warehouses, shops and data centers, actively picked across the property sector. It is built for rent-based income and property exposure without buying buildings, and it tends to fall when interest rates rise because borrowing costs shape property values.
TRUU: Utility companies: the regulated providers of electricity, gas and water, actively picked across the sector. Utilities are a classic defensive holding, paying steady dividends and usually moving less than the market, though they tend to lag when interest rates rise.
TSIE: Securitized bonds: pools of mortgages and other loans packaged into bonds that pay interest from the payments flowing in. It is an income fund built on loan pools rather than company or government debt, so its risks hinge on borrowers keeping up with their payments.
TSLW: An income strategy wrapped around one stock, Tesla, the electric car maker, using options and Treasury bills rather than simply holding shares. It aims to pay distributions weekly, and the trade-off is that everything rides on one famously volatile stock, with options capping some of its biggest jumps.
TYYY: An income fund built around Tesla stock exposure, held mostly in cash and Treasury bills while options and other instruments provide the link to the shares. It aims to pay income frequently, but everything depends on one volatile stock, so it is a speculation tool rather than a steady holding.
UBIQ: Companies in the US e-commerce ecosystem: online retailers, marketplaces and the payment and delivery firms that online shopping runs on. It is a focused bet on shopping continuing to move online, so it leans consumer and technology heavy and swings with consumer spending.
USMD: US technology companies chosen for their importance to American innovation, security and industrial strength, with technology at about two-thirds and industrials making up most of the rest. It is an actively managed growth bet with a patriotic screen, so it leans into defense-adjacent and strategic tech rather than owning the whole sector.
XIGV: One hundred big US technology companies with software deliberately left out, leaving chipmakers, hardware firms and other non-software tech. It is a more physical slice of the tech sector, so it leans on the chip cycle and device demand rather than on subscription software growth.
XOEX: The big US companies of the S&P 100 with the twenty largest deliberately removed, leaving the next tier of blue chips across industries. Cutting out the giants makes it less top-heavy than a normal large-company fund, so it behaves like a mildly contrarian core holding.
XX: A defined-outcome bet that the S&P 500 reaches 10,000 by 2030, built with options that behave like one long call on the index. If the index gets there early it can pay off handsomely, but if 2030 arrives below the target the options can expire worthless, so it is an all-or-nothing wager.
